title: The History of Iran: Every Empire, Every Invasion
text: Persepolis, 330 BC. The palace of the Persian kings is burning, set alight by a Macedonian conqueror who has just destroyed the greatest empire the world had yet seen. Nearly two thousand three hundred and fifty years later, in February 2026, American and Israeli missiles strike Tehran. Between these two fires lies the story of one of the oldest nations on Earth: a land invaded again and again by Greeks, Arabs, Turks, Mongols, Afghans, Russians, British and Americans, and yet a land that never stopped being Iran. So when was Iran born? Which rulers made it, and which conquerors broke it? And how many governments have ruled it? Let us begin at the beginning. Chapter one. The land of the Aryans. Iran is a high plateau, ringed by mountains: the Zagros in the west, the Alborz in the north, and great salt deserts at its heart. Its first civilisation was not Iranian at all. From around 3200 BC the Elamites built cities on the lowlands of Khuzestan, with Susa as their capital, and for two thousand years they traded and fought with Sumer and Babylon. Then, late in the second millennium BC, new peoples arrived from Central Asia. They called themselves Arya, the noble ones, and their land would one day be called Eran, the land of the Aryans. That word is the origin of the name Iran. The first of these peoples to build a kingdom were the Medes, around Ecbatana, modern Hamadan. In 612 BC their king, Cyaxares, allied with Babylon and destroyed Nineveh, the capital of the terrifying Assyrian Empire. The Medes now ruled from Anatolia to the edge of Central Asia. But their own vassal, a Persian prince from the south, was about to overtake them. Chapter two. Cyrus the Great. In 550 BC, Cyrus of Persis defeated his overlord, Astyages, king of the Medes, and took Ecbatana. Most historians date the birth of the first Iranian empire to this moment. What followed was one of the fastest conquests in history. In 547 BC Cyrus marched west and crushed Croesus of Lydia, the richest king of his age, taking Sardis. In 539 BC he entered Babylon, almost without a fight. Instead of burning the city, he honoured its gods, and he allowed the exiled Jews to return to Jerusalem and rebuild their temple. His proclamation survives on a clay barrel known as the Cyrus Cylinder. His son Cambyses added Egypt in 525 BC. Then came Darius the First, who turned conquest into government. He divided the empire into provinces called satrapies, built the Royal Road of more than two thousand five hundred kilometres from Sardis to Susa, introduced a gold coinage, and began the ceremonial capital of Persepolis. On the cliff of Behistun he carved his victories in three languages. Clay tablets found at Persepolis show the workers who built it, men and women alike, paid in grain, wine and silver. At its height the Achaemenid Empire stretched from the Balkans and Egypt to the Indus River, ruling perhaps two fifths of humanity. Only the Greeks resisted. At Marathon in 490 BC, and at Salamis in 480 BC, the armies and fleets of Darius and his son Xerxes were turned back. Persia remained the superpower of its age, but a Greek revenge was coming. Chapter three. Alexander. In 334 BC, Alexander of Macedon crossed into Asia with fewer than fifty thousand men. He won at the Granicus, then at Issus in 333 BC, where Darius the Third fled the field. In 331 BC, at Gaugamela, near modern Erbil, the last great Achaemenid army broke. Alexander took Babylon and Susa, and in 330 BC Persepolis burned. Darius was murdered by his own satrap while fleeing east. Two hundred and twenty years of Achaemenid rule were over. When Alexander died in 323 BC, his general Seleucus seized the eastern provinces, and for almost a century Iran was ruled by Greek kings. Chapter four. The Parthians. Around 247 BC a nomadic Iranian people called the Parni rose in the north east under their chief Arsaces. They became the Parthians. Under Mithridates the First they drove the Seleucids out of Iran and Mesopotamia, and built their capital at Ctesiphon on the Tigris. Their weapon was the horse archer. In 53 BC, at Carrhae, the Parthian general Surena destroyed a Roman army of seven legions and killed the triumvir Crassus. For nearly five centuries the Parthians held Rome at the Euphrates. But their kingdom was loose, a federation of great noble houses, and in the end it was overthrown from within. Chapter five. The Sasanians. In 224 AD, a Persian lord named Ardashir defeated and killed the last Parthian king, Artabanus the Fourth, at the battle of Hormozgan. He took the title King of Kings of Eran, and for the first time the name Eranshahr, the realm of the Iranians, was used for the state itself. His son Shapur the First humiliated Rome three times. In 260 AD, near Edessa, he captured the Roman emperor Valerian, the only Roman emperor ever taken alive by a foreign enemy, and carved the scene into the rock at Naqsh-e Rostam. Under Khosrow the First, called Anushirvan, the Sasanian state reached its golden age, with a reformed tax system, the great palace of Ctesiphon, and scholars from Greece and India at court. But his grandson, Khosrow the Second, fought a twenty six year war against Byzantium. His armies took Jerusalem, Alexandria and reached the walls of Constantinople, before the emperor Heraclius struck back and destroyed them. By 628 AD both empires were exhausted. They did not see the storm rising in the deserts of Arabia. Chapter six. The Arab conquest. In 636 AD, at Qadisiyyah, near the Euphrates, the Muslim army under Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas met the Sasanian host and its war elephants. After three days of fighting the Persian commander Rostam was dead. Ctesiphon fell the next year. In 642 AD, at Nahavand, the last imperial army was defeated, a battle the Arabs called the victory of victories. The last Sasanian king, Yazdegerd the Third, fled from city to city, until in 651 AD he was killed near Merv. Iran became part of the Caliphate, and over the next three centuries most Iranians embraced Islam. Yet Iran was not absorbed. Persian administrators ran the caliphs' treasuries, and the Abbasid revolution of 750 was launched from Khorasan. The Persian language survived, reborn in Arabic script, and around 1010 AD the poet Ferdowsi completed the Shahnameh, the Book of Kings, sixty thousand verses that preserved the memory of ancient Iran. Chapter seven. Iranian dynasties and Turkish swords. As the power of Baghdad faded, local dynasties rose. The Tahirids in Khorasan. The Saffarids of Sistan, founded by Ya'qub, a coppersmith turned warlord. The Samanids of Bukhara, patrons of Persian poetry. And the Buyids, who in 945 AD marched into Baghdad itself and ruled the caliph as their guest. Then came the Turks. Mahmud of Ghazni built an empire from Afghanistan, raiding deep into India seventeen times. In 1040, at Dandanaqan, the Seljuk Turks defeated the Ghaznavids, and in 1055 their leader Tughril Beg entered Baghdad as sultan. The Seljuks ruled from Isfahan, beat Byzantium at Manzikert in 1071, and their great Persian vizier, Nizam al-Mulk, built colleges across the empire. After them came the Khwarazmshahs, whose empire was vast, rich and arrogant. In 1218 their governor at Otrar massacred a caravan of merchants sent by Genghis Khan. Chapter eight. The Mongols and Timur. The answer came in 1219. Mongol armies stormed Otrar, Bukhara and Samarkand. In 1221 Merv and Nishapur were annihilated; Persian chroniclers wrote of hundreds of thousands dead, numbers no historian can confirm, but the destruction was real. Irrigation canals that had watered Khorasan for centuries were ruined. In 1256 Hulagu Khan, grandson of Genghis, destroyed the fortress of Alamut, and in 1258 he sacked Baghdad, ending the Abbasid Caliphate. Hulagu founded the Ilkhanate, a Mongol state centred on Tabriz, and in 1295 his descendant Ghazan converted to Islam. A century later came a new conqueror, Timur, known in the West as Tamerlane. In the 1380s he took Herat, Tabriz and Shiraz. When Isfahan rebelled in 1387 his soldiers built towers from the skulls of its people; the chronicles speak of seventy thousand. After Timur, Turkmen confederations, the Black Sheep and the White Sheep, fought over the ruins. Chapter nine. The Safavids. In 1501, a fourteen year old boy named Ismail, leader of the Safavid order, entered Tabriz with his Qizilbash warriors and was crowned Shah. He made Twelver Shia Islam the religion of the state, and in doing so drew borders of faith that still separate Iran from its neighbours. Many historians see this as the birth of modern Iran. In 1514, at Chaldiran, Ottoman cannons under Sultan Selim the First destroyed the Qizilbash cavalry and took Tabriz, and for a century Iran fought for its life between the Ottomans and the Uzbeks. Then came Shah Abbas the Great, who ruled from 1588 to 1629. He built a modern army with muskets and artillery, retook Tabriz and Baghdad, and in 1622, with English ships, expelled the Portuguese from Hormuz. He made Isfahan his capital, with its great square, its blue domed mosques and its bridges. Persians said Isfahan is half the world. Persian painting, carpets and silk reached their height, and European envoys, like the English adventurers Anthony and Robert Sherley, came to Isfahan seeking an alliance against the Ottomans. Chapter ten. Afghans and Nader Shah. By 1722 the Safavid state had grown weak. An Afghan army of perhaps twenty thousand under Mahmud Hotak defeated the Persian army at Gulnabad and besieged Isfahan for six months. Tens of thousands starved, and the Shah surrendered his crown. Iran was rescued by a soldier of genius from Khorasan, Nader of the Afshar tribe. He drove out the Afghans, threw back the Ottomans and the Russians, and in 1736 crowned himself Shah. Then he turned east. In 1739, at Karnal, he crushed the Mughal army and entered Delhi. When a riot broke out, his troops massacred thousands of its people. He returned home with the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor diamond. Historians have called him the Napoleon of Persia, the last great conqueror of Asia, and of all Iran's rulers his campaigns are the most famous. But Nader grew cruel and suspicious, and in 1747 his own officers murdered him in his tent. After him, Karim Khan Zand ruled most of Iran from Shiraz and refused the title of Shah, calling himself only the Vakil, the representative of the people. Chapter eleven. The Qajars and the Great Game. In 1789 a eunuch prince of the Qajar tribe, Agha Mohammad Khan, began to reunite Iran by force. He made Tehran his capital, and in 1796 he was crowned Shah. But a new kind of enemy had arrived: European empires with modern armies. In two wars Russia defeated Iran. By the treaties of Gulistan in 1813 and Turkmenchay in 1828, Iran lost Georgia, Dagestan, and the lands that are today Azerbaijan and Armenia. When Iran tried to retake Herat, Britain landed troops in the Persian Gulf, and in 1857 Iran gave up its claim. Iran was never colonised, but it was squeezed between Russia in the north and British India in the south. In 1906 a Constitutional Revolution forced the Shah to accept a parliament, the Majlis. A year later Britain and Russia divided Iran into spheres of influence without even asking its government. Chapter twelve. The Pahlavis. In 1921 an army officer named Reza Khan marched on Tehran with his Cossack brigade. In 1925 parliament deposed the last Qajar Shah, and Reza became Shah of a new dynasty, the Pahlavis. He built railways, schools and a national army. And in 1935 he asked foreign governments to stop calling his country Persia and to use the name its people had always used: Iran. But in 1941, during the Second World War, British and Soviet armies invaded to secure the oil fields and a supply route to Russia. Reza Shah was forced to abdicate in favour of his son, Mohammad Reza. In 1951 the elected Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh nationalised the oil industry. Two years later, in August 1953, a coup backed by the American CIA and British intelligence overthrew him. The Shah returned with full power, and an alliance with the United States, but resentment grew. Chapter thirteen. Revolution and war. In January 1979, after a year of mass protests, the Shah left Iran forever. On the first of February, Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini returned from exile in Paris, and in April a referendum declared an Islamic Republic. In November, students seized the American embassy and held fifty two Americans hostage for four hundred and forty four days. Then, on the twenty second of September 1980, Saddam Hussein's Iraq invaded. The war lasted eight years. Cities like Khorramshahr were fought over street by street, and in the War of the Cities, Iraqi missiles fell on Tehran. It brought trench warfare and chemical weapons, and killed hundreds of thousands of people, before a ceasefire in August 1988 left the borders unchanged. Chapter fourteen. The American wars. For the next three decades, Iran's nuclear programme and its alliances across the region set it against the United States and Israel. In June 2025, after Israel struck Iran, American bombers hit the nuclear sites of Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan. Then, on the twenty eighth of February 2026, the United States and Israel launched a joint war: Operation Epic Fury. The opening strikes killed Iran's Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, and many senior commanders. Iran answered with missiles and drones against Israel and American bases across the Gulf, and closed the Strait of Hormuz, sending oil prices soaring. On the eighth of March, the Assembly of Experts chose his son, Mojtaba Khamenei, as the new Supreme Leader. In April, Pakistan brokered a ceasefire and hosted the first face to face talks between America and Iran in forty seven years. The talks ended without a deal, and the United States blockaded Iran's ports. A memorandum signed in June raised hopes of peace, but in July the ceasefire collapsed in the Strait. In November 2026 American aircraft struck air defences on the island of Qeshm, and the war that began in February is still not over. Epilogue. So, how many governments has Iran had? Counting only the major ruling houses, from the Medes to the Islamic Republic, more than twenty: Medes, Achaemenids, Seleucids, Parthians, Sasanians, the Caliphs, Tahirids, Saffarids, Samanids, Buyids, Ghaznavids, Seljuks, Khwarazmshahs, Ilkhans, Timurids, Turkmen, Safavids, Hotaks, Afsharids, Zands, Qajars, Pahlavis, and the Islamic Republic. The exact number depends on how you count. When was Iran founded? Its first empire in 550 BC; its name as a state under the Sasanians; its modern borders and faith under the Safavids in 1501. Many conquered it: Alexander, the Arabs, the Turks, Genghis Khan and Timur. Yet every time, the conquerors ended up speaking Persian, reading Ferdowsi, and ruling as Shahs. Plutarch records the words said to be written on the tomb of Cyrus at Pasargadae. O man, whoever you are and wherever you come from, I am Cyrus, who won the Persians their empire. Do not begrudge me this little earth that covers my body. Twenty five centuries later, the empires that came to Iran are dust. Iran is still there, and its story is not finished.
